newsitem.title: USA: AT&T launches trial on new Web service.
newsitem.headline: AT&T launches trial on new Web service.

text.p: AT&T said Tuesday it is launching a trial program allowing surfers of the World Wide Web to request nearly instantaneous telephone calls from businesses that advertise on the Internet.
Five companies will be participating in the trial, which is to begin in October and run through the end of the year, to help AT&T work out the kinks and to how much it would charge for the service.
The new technology, called Instant Answers, will allow individuals to click on an icon on a company's homepage to request a call from a sales representative or service agent.
It would be offered to customers of AT&T's 800-number business. The company said it hopes that businesses that use AT&T's toll-free service also will seek to have AT&T host their Web sites.
AT&T, which held a telephone conference call Tuesday on the new service, said they hoped it would allow businesses to offer a more personal touch in communicating with customers over the Internet.
"The human touch is noticeably missing" from the Internet in its current form, said David Nagel, president of AT&T Laboratories.

For example, customers who tap into the homepage for TeleService Resources will be able to view rooms listed under Small Luxury Hotels of the World. Based on the images flashed on the computer screen, a customer could then ask for an immediate call from TeleServices and reserve a room.
"E-mailing just can't provide that type of instant gratification," said Kathleen Earley, vice president of AT&T EasyCommerce Services.
Neither the companies participating in the new service, nor the customers who link up to their Web pages will need any special software, AT&T said.
The company said it anticipates businesses that use the service will be charged on a per-transaction basis, though no rate has been established yet.

AT&T said the trial will, among other things, help the company determine how businesses could guard against Web sufers maliciously asking for frequent telephone calls -- usage that would drive up their costs if they are charged on a per-transaction basis.
"Those are the kind of service functions ... we'll be shaking out," Earley said.

Besides TeleService, the companies participating in the trial are: Consumer Car Club of San Francisco; Roche Diagnostic Systems of Branchburg, N.J.; Stahls' Inc of St. Claire Shores, Mich; and Personal Mortgage Corp of Brewster, N.Y.
